title: Negotiating Rent in India: How to Get a Better Deal Without Losing the Flat
seoTitle: How to Negotiate Rent in India
description: What is really negotiable when you rent in India, the exact words to use, what to offer in return, and the times when pushing will cost you the flat.
excerpt: Rent is the stickiest number in the deal and the only one most people try to move. Here is what actually shifts, what to say, and when to say nothing at all.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: Renters who have negotiated well, and badly

faq.q: Is rent actually negotiable in India, or is the listed price fixed?
faq.a: It is usually negotiable, but rent moves less easily than everything else in the deal. A listed rent is an opening position, often set by looking at what neighbours are asking. The deposit, maintenance, lock-in, notice period and painting-on-exit clause all tend to move more readily than the monthly rent, because they cost the owner less to give away.

faq.q: How much should I ask for?
faq.a: Name a specific number rather than asking whether the price is negotiable, because the second question has one easy answer. Base the number on the total monthly cost you worked out for comparable flats nearby, not on a percentage rule. Then stop talking and let the owner respond.

faq.q: What is the easiest thing to negotiate?
faq.a: The deposit, and small repairs before you move in. Reducing the deposit costs the owner nothing in income since it is money they hold and return, while reducing rent costs them every month of the tenancy. Repairs are one-time and cheap for the owner compared with another vacant month.

When the owner has several people viewing the same week, the listing is new and sharply priced, or someone else is already asking about paperwork. In that situation the owner loses nothing by saying no to you. Ask only for things that cost them nothing, such as a repair or a written clause, or take it at the asking price.

faq.q: The owner agreed to something verbally. Is that enough?
faq.a: No. A verbal concession is worth nothing at move-out, when memories differ and the person you agreed with may not be the person handling your exit. Ask for every agreed point to be written into the agreement, including the deposit amount and refund timeline, who pays for painting on exit, what is included in maintenance, and any repairs promised before move-in.

faq.q: Can I negotiate at renewal, or only when moving in?
faq.a: Renewal is often the easier conversation. Replacing you costs the owner a vacant month or more, possible brokerage, repainting, and the risk of an unknown tenant, all to replace someone who has paid on time. Open the discussion six to eight weeks before renewal, and check first whether your agreement already fixes a revision percentage.

body:
Two flats in the same Kondapur building, same floor plan, one above the other. Neha pays 24,000 a month. The man in 3B pays 27,000 for an identical layout — same tiles, same age, same view of the same water tank. He moved in four months before she did.

He isn't careless with money. He's an engineer who reads the fine print on his phone bill. He just did what almost everyone does: heard a number, decided he could afford it, and said yes.

Neha asked one question. "I like it and I can move in on the 1st. If I sign for two years, what's the best you can do?" The owner was quiet for maybe six seconds, said 24,000, and that was that. Six seconds of somebody else's thinking, and a difference of 36,000 a year.

She didn't argue. She didn't have a strategy. She asked, once, and then stopped talking.

That's most of what this article is about — but not all of it, because there are also flats where asking that same question would have lost her the place, and knowing which is which matters more than any script.

## Why almost nobody negotiates

Three reasons, and all three are understandable.

**It feels rude.** Renting a home in India is personal. You're standing in somebody's flat, they're telling you about the water supply and their last tenant, and haggling feels like haggling over a gift. But you're not negotiating with a friend. You're negotiating the price of something you'll pay for every month for years, and the owner doesn't think it's rude. They've had this conversation before.

**People assume the price is fixed.** It usually isn't. A listed rent is an opening position, often set by looking at what the neighbours are asking, or by what the last tenant paid plus something. It's a guess, not a valuation.

**Fear of losing the flat.** Sometimes correct, which is why this article has a section on when to keep your mouth shut. But mostly the fear is out of proportion. An owner who has spent a month showing an empty flat won't throw you out for asking a polite question.

## What's actually negotiable, ranked by how often it moves

Rent is what everyone fixates on, and it's the hardest thing to move. Here's roughly the order I'd try, softest first.

**The deposit.** The most flexible thing in the entire deal and the one nobody asks about. Think about why: reducing the deposit costs the owner nothing in income. It's money they hold and return. Reducing rent costs them every single month for as long as you stay. An owner who won't drop rent by 1,000 will often drop the deposit by a month without much thought — and a month's deposit is a much bigger number sitting in your bank account today. If you understand the rules and the refund protocol before you ask, you'll ask better; that's covered separately in [security deposits in India](/blog/security-deposits-in-india).

**Maintenance.** Sometimes a fixed society charge the owner can't touch. Sometimes a number the owner invented. Always worth asking who actually pays it and whether it's included. This one is easy to get wrong because it's small monthly and large annually.

**The lock-in period.** Owners like long lock-ins because vacancy is their real cost. If you're confident about staying, a longer lock-in is the cheapest thing you can give away. If you're not confident, a shorter lock-in is worth real money to you — see [breaking a lease in India](/blog/breaking-a-lease-in-india) for what it costs when a lock-in bites.

**The notice period.** Often movable by a month, and it costs the owner very little while you're a good tenant.

**Painting on exit.** A clause that says the tenant pays for repainting is extremely common and quietly expensive. It's also one of the most negotiable clauses in the whole agreement, because owners know it's a sore point. Ask for it to be removed, capped at a fixed amount, or made conditional on actual damage.

**Parking.** Often charged separately, often available, often thrown in if you ask at the right moment.

**Repairs before move-in.** A geyser that works, a leaking tap, a rattling fan, a missing mosquito mesh. Owners usually agree, because these are one-time and cheap next to a vacant month. It's the easiest "yes" in the conversation and a good thing to ask for first.

**Furnishing.** Adding a wardrobe or a fridge, or removing furniture you don't want and the rent that comes with it.

**Rent itself.** Stickiest, because it's the number the owner has emotionally settled on, the number they quote to relatives, and the number that resets their expectations for the next tenant. It moves most when the flat has been empty.

### The trade table

| What to ask for | How often it moves | What to offer in return |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lower deposit | Often — the least-asked, most flexible item | A longer lock-in, or rent paid on a fixed early date each month |
| Small repairs before move-in | Almost always | Nothing. Ask early, ask plainly |
| Maintenance included in rent | Sometimes, if the owner set the number | Taking the flat as-is, no repainting |
| Painting-on-exit clause removed or capped | Often | Agreeing to a professional deep clean at exit instead |
| Shorter lock-in | Sometimes | A higher deposit, or a longer notice period |
| Longer notice period for you | Often | A longer notice period for them too |
| Parking included | Sometimes | Moving in immediately |
| Lower rent | Least often, and only with real leverage | A two-year commitment, immediate move-in, or a higher deposit |

## The leverage you actually have

Leverage is just the answer to one question: what does saying yes to you get the owner that saying no doesn't?

**An empty flat.** This is the big one. Every vacant month is money the owner will never recover, and it's already gone by the time you're standing there. Signs: dust on the sills, no curtain rods, the electricity meter reading almost nothing, a watchman who says nobody's lived there since March. Ask directly — "how long has it been vacant?" — and listen to how fast they answer.

**Timing.** Owners have their own deadlines: a loan EMI, a move abroad, a month-end they've been dreading. You won't know it, but you'll feel it in how fast they reply.

**A longer commitment.** Vacancy and turnover are the owner's biggest costs. Two years of a reliable tenant is worth real money to them.

**Looking low-risk.** This is underrated. Salary slips ready, a stable job, a previous owner willing to vouch for you, a household profile that matches what they've said they want, documents already in a folder on your phone. Owners are pricing risk as much as space, and organised paperwork lowers the price of that risk before you say a word about money.

**Being able to move immediately.** "I can shift on the 1st" is a real concession. It ends their vacancy today.

**Being willing to walk.** Only if it's true. More on that below.

## The leverage you don't have

Pretending you have leverage you don't is worse than having none, because the owner can tell.

- **"I saw a cheaper flat in Madhapur."** Different area, different product, and they know it. If you'd rather have the cheaper flat, take it.
- **Threatening to walk when you've spent twenty minutes saying how much you love the balcony.** You've already told them.
- **Criticising the flat as a tactic.** Pointing out real problems is fine. Manufacturing complaints to justify a lower number reads as bad faith, and you're about to depend on this person to fix your geyser.
- **Quoting an "average rent" from a website.** Nobody in the room believes it, including you.
- **Rushing.** If your current lease ends in eight days and you've said so, you have no leverage at all.

## Do the homework: compare total cost, not headline rent

The single most useful thing you can do before negotiating is to work out what each flat actually costs per month, all in. A flat at 22,000 with 3,000 maintenance, separate parking and a summer water tanker bill can be more expensive than one at 25,000 with everything included.

Add up rent, maintenance, parking, likely water and electricity, and any one-time costs spread over how long you'll actually stay — brokerage, if you're paying it, is commonly quoted in months of rent and varies a lot by city and by how hard you push. [The hidden costs of renting in India](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india) has the full list.

Then you're not guessing. You know maintenance is where the money is on this particular flat, and you can ask for the thing that matters instead of reflexively pushing on rent.

## The conversation itself

**Have it after you've seen the flat, not before.** On the phone, before a viewing, you're a stranger with a question. Standing in the living room, having said you like it, you're a solution to their problem.

**Do it in person or on a call. Not over text.** Saying no over WhatsApp is free — no pause, no tone, no person in front of them. On a call, silence does work for you that a typed message can't. If a text conversation is all you have, at least call to close it.

**Signal you're serious first, then ask.** The order matters enormously.

> "I like it, and honestly this is the one I'd take. I can move in on the 1st and I'd sign for two years. If I do that, what's the best you can do on the rent?"

**Name a number.** Do not ask "is this negotiable?" That question has one easy answer and it's no. A specific number forces a specific reply and gives the owner something to counter.

> "Would you consider 24,000?"

> "Can we do two months' deposit instead of three? Everything else exactly as you've said."

> "If I take it as-is and don't ask you to repaint, could we do 23,500?"

**Then stop talking.** This is the hardest part and the most effective. Most people ask, get uncomfortable in the pause, and start negotiating against themselves — "but I mean, obviously, if that doesn't work I understand, we could do 26,000 —". Let the silence sit. Count to ten in your head if you have to.

**Make one bundled ask, not six separate ones.** A list of demands feels like a negotiation with a difficult person. One clear ask feels like a deal.

**Know where you stop.** Decide your number before you walk in. If they meet it, say yes immediately and warmly. Grinding for another 500 after they've moved is how goodwill evaporates on day zero, and you're about to spend two years asking this person for favours.

## Trade instead of asking

Every ask is easier to say yes to when it's attached to something.

- A longer lock-in for a lower rent.
- A higher deposit for a lower monthly rent — good for you if you're staying long and have the cash, bad if you're not sure.
- A lower deposit for slightly higher rent — good if cash today matters more than cash per month.
- Taking the flat as-is, no repainting, no fixes, in exchange for a number.
- A slightly longer notice period, which costs you little and reduces their vacancy risk.

Be careful with one common suggestion: paying several months of rent up front. It can genuinely move a price, but it also means handing over a large sum to someone you've just met, sometimes before an agreement exists. If you go that route, do it only after the agreement is signed, and read [how rental scams work in India](/blog/rental-scams-in-india) first.

The deposit is worth one specific note. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 recommends capping a residential security deposit at two months' rent — but it's a *model* law. It binds nobody until a state enacts its own version, and most haven't. So it isn't a rule you can cite at an owner. What it is, occasionally, is a useful reference point: "I've seen two months suggested as the standard — could we do that?" is a softer way to ask than naming your own preference.

## Get it in writing, or it didn't happen

This is where negotiations quietly die. The owner agrees over chai that they'll repaint before you move in, that the deposit comes back within thirty days, that painting on exit is on them. Nobody writes it down. Two years later there's no chai, sometimes no same owner, and definitely no record.

A verbal concession is worth exactly nothing at move-out.

So close every agreed point the same way:

> "That's great — can we put that line in the agreement? Just so neither of us has to remember it in two years."

That sentence is not confrontational. It's the most reasonable thing in the world, and an owner who refuses has told you something important about the next two years. Specifics you want written in: the exact deposit amount and the refund timeline, who pays for painting on exit, whether maintenance is included, what the lock-in and notice periods are, and any repairs promised before move-in with a date. [Rental agreements in India](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india) covers what the document should contain.

## When not to negotiate at all

Sometimes you have no leverage, and pushing will simply cost you the flat.

You'll know it when you see it: the owner is showing the place to four people the same afternoon, the listing went up two days ago and is priced sharply, someone else is already asking about the paperwork, or the building has a waiting list. In a hot micro-market, the owner's cost of saying no to you is zero. They'll have another tenant by Thursday.

In that situation, either take it at the asking price and take it fast, or ask only for things that cost the owner nothing — a repair, a written clause, a small fix. Don't touch the rent. And if you genuinely can't afford it, don't negotiate; go and look somewhere else, because you were never going to get this one.

The other time not to negotiate: when you haven't decided you want the flat. Negotiating a price you're not prepared to accept wastes everyone's afternoon and burns the goodwill you'd need if you changed your mind.

## Renewal is a different, easier conversation

Most people accept a renewal hike without a word, which is odd, because renewal is usually the moment your leverage is highest.

Look at it from the owner's side. If you leave, they face an empty month or two, a possible broker, repainting, cleaning, new-tenant risk, and the whole hassle of showing the flat to strangers. All of that to replace someone who has paid on time for two years and never called at midnight. Losing you is genuinely expensive for them.

So open the conversation early — six to eight weeks before renewal, before they've committed to a number in their own head. And lead with the thing that's true.

> "I'd like to stay another two years. I've enjoyed living here and I've never been late. Can we keep the rent where it is this time?"

Or, if a hike is coming:

> "I understand a revision — would you consider half of what you've proposed if I commit for two years?"

Check what your existing agreement says first. Many write in a fixed revision percentage at renewal, in which case you're negotiating against a document rather than a mood, and you should know that before you start.

## When to walk away

Walk when the total monthly cost stops making sense against your budget — not the headline rent, the real number. Walk when the owner won't put an agreed point in writing. Walk when the negotiation itself is unpleasant, because how someone behaves over 1,000 rupees is a preview of how they'll behave over your deposit. And walk when you've stretched: a flat you can only afford if nothing goes wrong is a flat you'll resent by month four.

Have somewhere else to walk to. That's really what leverage is. See three more places before you commit to one — [a house-hunting checklist](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india) helps you keep them straight — and negotiate from a position where "no" is survivable.

---

## Where StayOnMap fits

Two small things that make this easier.

You talk to the owner directly. There's no intermediary in the middle whose commission is calculated as a share of the rent you're trying to bring down, and no brokerage to pay.

And rent, deposit and maintenance are required fields on every listing, so you can compare the real monthly cost of three flats before you're standing in any of them — which is the homework this whole article depends on. What you do with the conversation is still up to you.

---

Neha's neighbour in 3B found out about the 24,000 eventually, the way people do — a conversation in the lift. He was annoyed for about a week. What bothered him wasn't the money, he said later. It was that he'd never asked.

Ask. Once, politely, with a number in it. And then be quiet.

Still working out what to ask on the viewing itself? Start with [the questions to ask before renting](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting).
